problem: Calculate the point where the ellipse  ${x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+2\sqrt{2}x+8y+2=0$ intercepts the $x$-axis.

examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the x-Intercepts of an Ellipse By Completing the Square

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095453/assets/4527514f6b522bf5922bcba4b77a1574b29f65c238c8b3dd976d6af6bb6c01ae.png)

Calculate the points where the ellipse $x^2 + 3y^2 - 4x -  6y = 2$ (shown above) intercepts the $x$-axis.
examples.worked_solution:
To calculate the $x$-intercepts, we need to substitute $y = 0$ into the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $x.$ We do this and solve the resulting equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}-4x-6y & =2 \\ {x}^{2}+3\cdot {0}^{2}-4x-6\cdot 0 & =2 \\ {x}^{2}-4x & =2 \\ ({x}^{2}-4x+4)-4 & =2 \\ (x-2)^{2}-4 & =2 \\ (x-2)^{2} & =6 \\ x-2 & =\pm \sqrt{6} \\ x & =2\pm \sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $x$-axis at $(2-\sqrt{6},0)$ and $(2+\sqrt{6},0).$

feedback.problem: Calculate the point where the ellipse $\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{16}+\frac{(y-7)^{2}}{9}=1$ intercepts the $x$-axis.
feedback.worked_solution:
To calculate the $x$-intercept, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the ellipse and solve the resulting equation for $x.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{16}+\frac{(y-7)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+3)^{2}}{16}+\frac{(0-7)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ \frac{(x+3)^{2}}{16}+\frac{49}{9} & =1 \\ 9(x+3)^{2}+(49\cdot 16) & =9\cdot 16 \\ 9(x+3)^{2}+784 & =144 \\ 9(x+3)^{2} & =-640 \\ (x+3)^{2} & =-\frac{640}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(x+3)^{2}\ge 0$, there is no $x$ such that $(x+3)^{2}=-\frac{640}{9}.$ Therefore, the ellipse has no $x$-intercepts, meaning that it does not intercept the $x$-axis at any point.
